units.t: Thought Experiments. Episode one.

In this episode: The trolley problem: would you pull the lever, The ship of Theseus: what makes you the same person, The ring of Gyges: would you be good if no one could see and The experience machine: would you plug in.
Part one. The trolley problem: would you pull the lever.
A runaway tram, five people on the track and one lever in your hand.
This simple puzzle has become one of the most argued-about scenarios in moral philosophy, and it now shapes how we think about self-driving cars.
The puzzle.
Picture yourself beside a railway line.
A tram with failed brakes is hurtling towards five workers who cannot get out of the way.
You stand next to a lever.
Pull it, and the tram swings onto a side track, where it will kill one worker instead.
Do nothing, and five people die.
Most people say they would pull the lever.
But the puzzle is not really about trams.
It is a carefully built thought experiment, a stripped-down scenario that isolates one question so we can examine our moral instincts.
Do the numbers alone matter, or does how a death comes about matter too?
The British philosopher Philippa Foot introduced it in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson later named it and invented many variations.
The footbridge twist.
Thomson's most famous variation puts you on a footbridge above the track.
There is no lever.
The only way to stop the tram is to push a very large stranger off the bridge into its path.
His body would halt it, saving five, but he would die.
The arithmetic is identical: one life for five.
Yet in surveys, most people who would pull the lever say they would not push the man.
Many find pushing deeply wrong, even if they struggle to explain why.
That gap makes the puzzle so productive.
If the numbers are the same, something else must be driving our judgement, and philosophers have spent decades working out what it is, and whether it should count.
The case for counting.
One family of answers is consequentialism: the rightness of an action depends on its results.
The best-known version, utilitarianism, associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, aims for the greatest overall wellbeing.
In the lever case, five deaths are worse than one, so you should pull.
A consistent consequentialist may say the same about the footbridge, arguing our reluctance to push is a gut reaction, not a moral insight.
Defenders note the approach is impartial and takes every life equally seriously.
Critics reply that if outcomes are all that matter, it could justify terrible things, such as harvesting one healthy patient's organs to save five others, which almost everyone rejects.
The case for limits.
A rival tradition, linked to Immanuel Kant, holds that people must never be treated merely as a means to an end.
Pushing the man uses his body as a tool to stop the tram, which looks like exactly that.
Pulling the lever is different: the one worker dies as a side effect of redirecting the threat, not as the means of stopping it.
This is the heart of the doctrine of double effect, which traces back to the medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas.
It says causing harm as a foreseen side effect can sometimes be permissible when causing the same harm intentionally would not.
Critics question whether that distinction can carry so much moral weight.
Brains and machines.
Around 2001, Joshua Greene and colleagues scanned people's brains as they considered trolley dilemmas.
Up-close, personal harms like pushing seemed to trigger stronger emotional responses, while impersonal cases like the lever invited calculation.
Greene proposed a 'dual process' account in which both systems compete.
Some later studies have questioned how well the results hold up, and philosophers ask whether the emotion tracks something real.
Then came autonomous vehicles.
Someone must decide in advance what software does when a crash is unavoidable.
The 2018 Moral Machine project from MIT collected millions of responses worldwide.
It found broad agreement on sparing more lives and humans over animals, but regional differences on other questions.
Engineers stress that real crashes are rarely neat dilemmas, and avoiding collisions is the goal.
The key idea: The trolley problem asks whether it is right to divert a runaway tram so it kills one person instead of five.
Part two. The ship of Theseus: what makes you the same person.
Replace every plank of a ship, one by one, and is it still the same ship?
This ancient puzzle leads straight to one of the most personal questions in philosophy: what makes you, you, over a lifetime of change?
A ship of new planks.
The Greek writer Plutarch, around the turn of the second century, told of the ship in which the hero Theseus was said to have sailed home from Crete.
The Athenians kept it for generations, removing old timbers as they decayed and fitting new ones.
Philosophers used it in arguments about growth: some said it stayed the same ship, others that it did not.
Carry the process to the end, with not one original plank left.
Is it still Theseus's ship?
If yes, what makes it so?
If no, at which plank did it stop being the original?
Neither answer is as comfortable as it first seems.
Hobbes's twist.
In the 1600s the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes added a complication.
Suppose someone collected every old plank as it was removed and later reassembled them, in order, into a ship.
Now there are two.
One sits in the harbour, continuously maintained, with no original material.
The other is built entirely of the original timbers.
Which is the ship of Theseus?
Both have a strong claim: one has continuity of history and use, the other continuity of material.
Our everyday idea of 'the same thing' bundles features that usually travel together but can come apart.
You are a ship too.
You are a bit like that ship.
Many of your cells are replaced over time, from skin to blood to the lining of your gut, although some, including most neurons in the brain, can last a lifetime.
Your beliefs, tastes and memories change even more.
The child in your earliest photos shares little with you in material, knowledge or personality, yet you feel certain that child was you.
Philosophers call this the problem of personal identity.
It matters for everyday things, like holding someone responsible for a promise or a crime, and for deeper ones, like what it would mean to survive.
Memory and its limits.
In the late 1600s John Locke argued that a person is a thinking being who can consider itself as itself at different times.
You are the same person as someone in the past if you remember that person's experiences from the inside, not because you share a body.
That explains why memory loss feels so frightening.
Nearly a century later, Thomas Reid offered the brave officer.
A boy is flogged for stealing; as an officer he remembers the flogging; as a general he remembers being the officer but has forgotten the flogging.
On Locke's view the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy.
Later philosophers repaired the theory with overlapping chains of memory and psychological connection.
Is there a fixed self.
Long before Locke, Buddhist thinkers took another route.
In the Questions of King Milinda, the monk Nagasena asks the king whether his chariot is the axle, the wheels, the frame or the reins.
None alone is the chariot, nor is it separate from them: 'chariot' names parts working together.
Likewise 'Nagasena' names a changing combination of body, feelings, perceptions and mental activity, with no unchanging core.
This idea, anatta or non-self, is central to many Buddhist traditions.
In 1984 Derek Parfit imagined a teleporter that destroys you and builds an exact copy on Mars.
Is that you?
He concluded there may be no fact of the matter, and that psychological continuity matters more than identity.
Many philosophers disagree.
The key idea: If every part of an object is gradually replaced, it is unclear whether it is still the same object.
Part three. The ring of Gyges: would you be good if no one could see.
A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, and soon he has seduced a queen and murdered a king.
Plato used the story to ask the most uncomfortable question in ethics.
A ring in a chasm.
Early in Plato's Republic, written around 375 BC, a young man named Glaucon tells a story.
A shepherd called Gyges is tending his flock in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, when an earthquake splits the ground.
In the chasm he finds a hollow bronze horse holding the body of a giant, wearing only a gold ring.
Gyges takes it.
Later he discovers that turning the ring's setting towards his palm makes him invisible, and turning it back makes him visible again.
He wastes no time.
He gets himself sent to the palace as a messenger, seduces the queen, kills the king with her help and takes the throne.
Glaucon's challenge.
Glaucon, one of Plato's older brothers, imagines two such rings: one given to a just man, one to an unjust man.
He bets that both would behave the same way, taking whatever they pleased.
Nobody is so iron-willed, he says, as to resist when there is no risk.
If so, justice is not valued for itself.
It is a compromise: we avoid harming each other because we fear being harmed.
He then raises the stakes.
A perfectly unjust man with a spotless reputation grows rich and admired, while a perfectly just man branded wicked is whipped, imprisoned and executed.
Which life is better?
Glaucon and his brother Adeimantus ask Socrates to prove that justice benefits the just person even when every outside reward is stripped away.
Socrates' long answer.
Answering the challenge takes up most of the rest of the Republic.
Socrates argues that the soul has three parts: reason, which seeks truth; spirit, which feels pride, anger and honour; and appetite, which craves food, sex and money.
In a just person, reason rules, spirit supports it and appetite is kept in its place.
In an unjust person, the parts are at war, and appetite or ambition takes control.
The unjust ruler with the magic ring is therefore not free at all.
He is a slave to cravings that can never be satisfied: restless, suspicious and alone.
Justice, Plato concludes, is to the soul what health is to the body, and no amount of wealth makes up for a sick soul.
Another Gyges.
Gyges may have been a real person.
A king of Lydia by that name ruled in the 7th century BC and founded a dynasty that later included the famously wealthy Croesus.
The historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, tells a very different tale of his rise.
King Candaules is so proud of his wife's beauty that he insists his bodyguard Gyges hide in the royal bedroom to see her undressed.
The queen spots him and gives him a stark choice: kill the king and marry her, or die.
He chooses the throne.
There is no magic ring in Herodotus, but both stories share hidden watching and power gained by stealth.
The test of the ring.
Readers often compare Gyges' ring to the One Ring in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, which also grants invisibility and corrupts its wearer.
Whether Tolkien had Plato in mind is uncertain.
Today many people carry a weaker version in their pockets: anonymous accounts, deleted messages and private browsing offer a taste of acting unseen.
The thought experiment lasts because it is so personal.
It asks not what rules a society needs, but what you would do if consequences vanished.
Try a small ring: a mistake in your favour at the till, an unwatched moment at work.
Some philosophers say Plato's answer merely redefines justice as inner balance.
Even so, the old saying holds: integrity is doing the right thing when no one is watching.
The key idea: In Plato's Republic, a shepherd finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seize a kingdom.
Part four. The experience machine: would you plug in.
Imagine a machine that could give you any life you wanted, every moment indistinguishable from reality.
Most people say they would refuse, and that refusal tells us something surprising about happiness.
A perfect simulation.
In 1974, the American philosopher Robert Nozick described a thought experiment in his book Anarchy, State, and Utopia.
Suppose brilliant neuroscientists could build a machine that stimulates your brain so you would think and feel you were writing a great novel, making a friend or reading an interesting book.
All the while you would actually be floating in a tank with electrodes attached to your head.
You could choose your experiences from a vast library, and you would not know you were plugged in.
Every moment would feel completely real.
Nozick even allowed for occasional breaks to choose the next stretch.
Then he asked: should you plug in for life?
Why most say no.
Many people, when first asked, say they would not plug in, even though the machine promises delight, achievement and love.
That reaction matters because of Nozick's target: hedonism, the view that pleasant experience is the only thing good in itself.
The 18th-century English philosopher Jeremy Bentham built his utilitarianism on the idea that pleasure and pain are all that ultimately matter.
If hedonism were true, the machine would be an easy choice, since it can deliver better feelings than real life ever could.
Hesitation suggests we value something beyond our own experiences.
If you feel a real but imperfect life beats a perfect simulated one, you are not a pure hedonist.
It became one of the most discussed thought experiments of the 20th century.
Doing, being and reality.
Nozick suggested three things the machine cannot give us.
First, we want to actually do certain things, not just have the experience of doing them.
We want to really write the novel, not merely feel as if we had.
Second, we want to be a certain kind of person.
In the tank you would be, as Nozick put it, an indeterminate blob, with no genuine courage, kindness or wit, because you never act.
Third, the machine limits us to a man-made reality, a world no deeper than its programmers imagined.
Plugging in, he wrote, is a kind of suicide.
Together these points suggest a good life involves real contact with the world and real achievement, not just good feelings.
The reversal.
Not everyone accepts Nozick's conclusion.
Some philosophers argue that our reluctance to plug in might reflect a bias towards the familiar, sometimes called status quo bias, rather than a deep truth about value.
To test this, the philosopher Felipe De Brigard reversed the scenario in a 2010 study.
He asked people to imagine discovering that they were already in an experience machine, and that their real life outside was very different.
Would they unplug?
Many said they would rather stay.
If people prefer to keep the life they know, real or simulated, then the original intuition may be less about reality and more about fear of losing what is familiar.
The debate continues.
What the machine reveals.
When The Matrix appeared in 1999, many viewers recognised Nozick's idea.
The character Cypher bites into a steak he knows is not real and decides he would rather return to the comfortable illusion.
Today virtual reality, immersive games and feeds tuned to our preferences offer partial versions of the machine.
None comes close, but each asks how much of your time you want to spend in experiences rather than reality.
The machine is useful because it separates what ordinary life bundles together: feeling good and doing good.
Some philosophers say well-being includes real relationships, knowledge and authenticity; others defend hedonism.
Either way, ask yourself: would you plug in?
If not, what would you miss?
Your answer summarises what you think life is for.
The key idea: Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you any experiences you wanted, indistinguishable from real life.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the trolley problem designed to test?
Answer. Whether numbers alone decide right, or the manner of a death counts too.
Question two. What difficulty does the ship of Theseus puzzle raise?
Answer. Whether an object stays the same after all its parts are replaced.
Question three. How does Gyges use the ring once he discovers its power?
Answer. He seduces the queen and takes the throne.
Question four. What does Nozick's experience machine do?
Answer. Makes chosen experiences feel real.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
